title: The Turmeric Co. Takes Turmeric Shots to UK Clinics to Fight 'Pain Pandemic'
excerpt: The functional-shot brand founded by ex-footballer Thomas Robson-Kanu is partnering healthcare practitioners across the UK to reach patients needing preventive solutions for inflammation and pain — putting Ayurveda's best-known root at the centre of a mainstream healthcare conversation.
body:
• The Turmeric Co., founded in 2018 by former footballer Thomas Robson-Kanu, is partnering healthcare practitioners across the UK under a new healthcare strategy reported by NutraIngredients.
  • The goal: get its turmeric shots to patients who need preventive solutions for inflammation and pain before conditions add to the strain on the NHS — what the company calls a "pain pandemic."
  • Robson-Kanu has credited turmeric shots with aiding his recovery from a career-threatening knee injury, the brand's founding story.
  • The strategy follows advertising scrutiny: the ASA censured the brand over testimonials implying its shots could treat disease, underscoring how tightly supplement claims are policed in the UK.

A turmeric-shot brand founded by a former professional footballer is taking its products into British clinics. The Turmeric Co. is partnering healthcare practitioners across the UK to put its shots in the hands of patients who need preventive solutions for inflammation and pain — part of what the company describes as a nationwide "pain pandemic."

From football injury to functional shots

The Turmeric Co. was founded in 2018 by Thomas Robson-Kanu, the former West Bromwich Albion and Wales striker, who has credited turmeric shots with aiding his recovery from a career-threatening knee injury. That personal story — an athlete turning to a traditional root after conventional routes fell short — became the brand's founding narrative and its core product: small, concentrated turmeric juice shots sold as a daily functional drink.

The healthcare strategy

According to NutraIngredients, reporting on September 16, the brand's new strategy is to work directly with healthcare practitioners to reach patients who need preventive solutions to inflammation and pain before their conditions lead to a further burden on the NHS. It is a notable pivot: from sports nutrition and direct-to-consumer wellness toward a quasi-clinical channel, positioning the shots as a preventive tool rather than just a lifestyle product.

The framing is deliberate. Chronic pain and inflammation-related conditions are among the largest drivers of primary-care visits in Britain, and the NHS has been under sustained pressure. A brand that can credibly sit in the prevention conversation — rather than the treatment one — has a far larger addressable market.

The claims tightrope

That distinction matters because UK regulators police it aggressively. The Advertising Standards Authority censured The Turmeric Co. this year over its website's use of republished customer testimonials for its turmeric shots, in which selected words had been blurred. The ASA concluded the blurring did not remove the overall meaning: consumers were "effectively invited to fill in the omitted wording," and the testimonials were likely to be understood as claims that the supplements could prevent, treat or cure human disease.

"Supplements are classed as foods and our rules make clear that ads can't make claims that a food can prevent, treat or cure a human disease or condition," an ASA spokesperson said. An earlier ruling in 2021 had already found a Facebook post for the brand in breach of the same rules.

This is the context in which the healthcare strategy must be read: the company cannot legally claim its shots treat pain, but it can work with practitioners on prevention and general wellness — provided the claims stay within the authorised register.

Building a science case

The brand has been investing in research to support its positioning. It previously ran a government-backed Knowledge Transfer Partnership with Nottingham Trent University — a 32-month research program testing its products' effects on hydration, inflammation, pain and recovery across demographics — and has planned studies on its turmeric shots' impact on inflammation, pain and recovery.

"The same regulatory bodies that deemed those drugs safe might restrict natural supplements that helped me manage my pain... Are we addressing the root cause of the health crisis?"

— Thomas Robson-Kanu, founder of The Turmeric Co.

For the diaspora, the story carries a familiar echo. Turmeric — haldi — has been a household staple across South Asia for centuries, from haldi doodh to cooking. The Turmeric Co.'s clinic push is, in a sense, Ayurveda's most famous ingredient completing its journey into the British mainstream: from grandmother's kitchen to the practitioner's shelf, via a footballer's knee.
nri_angle: For South Asian consumers in the UK who grew up on haldi doodh, The Turmeric Co.'s clinic push is Ayurveda's most familiar ingredient going mainstream through a healthcare front door.
